wstep: NCHFP research confirmed that garlic-in-oil mixtures stored at room temperature are at risk of botulism; this card describes the NCHFP instructions under which garlic in oil may be frozen for long-term storage, for up to several months.

ostrzezenia.tekst: Do not store garlic in oil at room temperature: low acidity, no free oxygen in the oil and warmth are ideal conditions for Clostridium botulinum to grow and produce toxin; the same applies to other low-acid foods in oil, such as herbs and chili peppers.

JarAtlas rule (cautious): freezing does not kill most bacteria, and the sources do not say how long thawed garlic in oil can be kept, so thaw it only in the refrigerator, only the portion you will use right away, and throw away any leftovers.

akapity: Make garlic in oil fresh.
If you are not freezing it, keep it in the refrigerator at 40 °F (4.4 °C) or lower for no more than 4 days.
Keeping garlic in oil in the refrigerator for longer than 4 days may allow Clostridium botulinum to grow.
According to Oregon State University Extension, peeled garlic pureed with oil, using 2 parts oil to 1 part garlic, should be frozen immediately and not held at room temperature.
Package garlic in oil in glass freezer jars or plastic freezer boxes, leaving 1/2 inch (about 1.3 cm) headspace, then label, date and freeze.
If you use glass, choose wide-mouth jars made for freezing and canning, because regular glass jars break easily at freezer temperatures.
According to Oregon State University Extension, crushed vegetables and herbs in oil can be frozen in ice cube trays and then packed in airtight containers as ready seasoning portions.
According to the same publication, pack frozen flavored oils airtight, for example in small glass or plastic jars, so their aroma does not penetrate other foods in the freezer.
Label garlic in oil kept in the refrigerator with the preparation date and preferably also a “discard after” date, that is 4 days later.
Freeze at 0 °F (−18 °C) or lower.
To speed up freezing, set the freezer to −10 °F (about −23 °C) or lower about 24 hours in advance.
Do not overload the freezer: add only as much unfrozen food as will freeze within 24 hours.
Keep the freezer at 0 °F (−18 °C) or lower, because at higher temperatures food loses quality faster; keep a freezer thermometer in it and check it often.
According to the FDA, freezing does not kill most bacteria; it only stops them from growing.
According to the NCHFP, garlic in oil can be kept in the freezer for up to several months.
Use the oldest packages first.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): the sources we read do not say how long garlic in oil can be kept after thawing, so thaw it only in the refrigerator and only as much as you will use right away.
Do not keep thawed leftovers; throw them away.
Never thaw food at room temperature or in warm water: its outer layer then warms into the danger zone of 40–140 °F (about 4–60 °C), where bacteria multiply rapidly.
Keep the refrigerator at 40 °F (4 °C) or lower.
Food is safe while it stays frozen, but once it thaws and warms above 40 °F (about 4 °C), bacteria present before freezing can start to multiply.
Appearance, smell and taste cannot tell you whether vegetables in oil carry a botulism hazard.
JarAtlas rule (cautious) after a freezer failure: throw away any package that has no ice crystals and is above 40 °F (about 4 °C), or that you cannot check.
The FDA also says to throw away perishable food that has been at room temperature for 2 hours or more, or 1 hour when it is above 90 °F (about 32 °C) outside.
